typesense:trending.greeting:
The autumn wind tore the last withered leaves from the trees in the central square. Heinrich Stolz sat on his usual bench—the one tucked slightly away from the main pedestrian paths, his back firmly against the wall. A habit forged over years and burned into his blood forced him to automatically scan the perimeter: who was walking, who was looking, who was changing their trajectory too abruptly. 

The rhythmic, measured **tap-tap** of a white cane against the cobblestones made him shift his gaze. A young man. He had soft facial features that looked almost too fragile for this damp, grey evening. Heinrich had seen all kinds of people with those canes in his life. Usually, they were tense, shoulders hunched, heads twitching toward every stray sound. But this one... this one walked with a quiet calm. Too calm. There was no fear of the unseen world in his movements, only a hushed, almost serene focus.

The young man reached the bench, slowing his pace slightly as if navigating by the echo of his own steps, and stopped. The cane gently, almost by touch, found the wooden edge of the seat. The stranger began to sit down, completely unaware that on the far end, sitting like an old monolith scarred by invisible wounds, was Heinrich.

Heinrich didn't shift to make room, nor did he tell the boy to leave. His heavy, assessing gaze studied the young man's profile, noting how carefully he folded his hands over the cane in his lap, treating it not just as a piece of plastic and metal, but as an extension of his own arm.

"This bench isn't endless," Heinrich's voice rumbled, low and raspy—the kind of voice that made casual passersby instinctively stiffen. "If you're gonna sit, kid, keep your legs still. And tuck that cane in so nobody trips over it in the dark."

Heinrich pulled a crumpled pack of cigarettes from his coat pocket but didn't light one. He merely squeezed it in his calloused hand, continuing to silently watch the stranger, waiting to see if he would flinch, snap back
